claim: ISWI-family nucleosome remodeling enzymes need the histone H4 N-terminal tail to mobilize nucleosomes.
source: ISWI-family nucleosome remodeling enzymes need the histone H4 N-terminal tail to mobilize nucleosomes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about ISWI enzymes.

claim: The H4-tail binding pocket of ISWI was mapped in this study.
source: Here we mapped the H4-tail binding pocket of ISWI.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The H4-tail binding site is adjacent to but not overlapping with the docking site of AutoN.
source: Surprisingly the binding site was adjacent to but not overlapping with the docking site of an auto-regulatory motif, AutoN, in the N-terminal region (NTR) of ISWI
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by crosslinking and modeling data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: AutoN does not act as a simple pseudosubstrate as suggested previously.
source: indicating that AutoN does not act as a simple pseudosubstrate as suggested previously.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that AutoN and H4 binding sites are adjacent but not overlapping, contradicting previous models.

claim: AutoN cooperates with AcidicN to confer H4-tail sensitivity.
source: Rather, AutoN cooperated with a hitherto uncharacterized motif, termed AcidicN, to confer H4-tail sensitivity and discriminate between DNA and nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by functional data showing that mutations in both AutoN and AcidicN reduce H4-tail dependence (Figure 8).

claim: AutoN and AcidicN cooperate to discriminate between DNA and nucleosomes.
source: Rather, AutoN cooperated with a hitherto uncharacterized motif, termed AcidicN, to confer H4-tail sensitivity and discriminate between DNA and nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase data showing that mutations in these motifs lead to loss of discrimination between DNA and chromatin (Figures 6, 7, 8).

claim: The ppHSA motif is functionally required in vivo.
source: A third motif in the NTR, ppHSA, was functionally required in vivo
evidence: This is demonstrated by yeast complementation assays showing that deletion of ppHSA fails to rescue growth defects (Figure 2).

claim: The ppHSA motif provides structural stability by clamping the NTR to Lobe 2 of the ATPase domain.
source: and provided structural stability by clamping the NTR to Lobe 2 of the ATPase domain.
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking data showing ppHSA contacts Lobe 2 (Figure 4, Table 1) and by the instability of ppHSA deletion mutants.

claim: The configuration of ISWI's NTR is reminiscent of Chd1 even though Chd1 contains an unrelated NTR.
source: This configuration is reminiscent of Chd1 even though Chd1 contains an unrelated NTR.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison showing that both NTR and Chd1 chromo domains dock to Lobe 2 in similar fashion (Figure 4).

claim: Nucleosomes consist of approximately 150 bp of DNA that wrap almost twice around an octamer of histones.
source: These particles consist of ~150 bp of DNA that wrap almost twice around an octamer of histones.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: Nucleosomal DNA is not accessible to most nuclear factors.
source: Nucleosomal DNA, however, is not accessible to most nuclear factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromatin structure and function.

claim: ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling complexes can alter the position or structure of nucleosomes.
source: Nature therefore evolved ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling complexes that can alter the position or the structure of nucleosomes as necessary.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromatin remodeling complexes.

claim: Some remodelers move nucleosomes along DNA, eject histones or exchange them for histone variants.
source: Some move nucleosomes along DNA, eject histones or exchange them for histone variants, and some can even perform several of these activities (Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Several remodelers respond to post-translational modifications present on histones.
source: Several remodelers, for instance, respond to post-translational modifications present on histones (Swygert and Peterson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swygert and Peterson, 2014.

claim: Some remodelers are directly regulated by post-translational modifications.
source: Others are directly regulated by post-translational modifications (Kim et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Some remodelers react to small signaling molecules.
source: or react to small signaling molecules (Zhao et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 1998.

claim: Cells adjust the subunit composition of remodeling complexes during development.
source: Cells also adjust the subunit composition of remodeling complexes during development (Lessard et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lessard et al., 2007.

claim: Mutations in subunits of human remodeling factors strongly associate with and in some cases drive cancers.
source: The fact that mutations in subunits of human remodeling factors strongly associate with and in some cases drive cancers underscores the necessity to regulate remodeler activity (Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015; Garraway and Lander, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015 and Garraway and Lander, 2013.

claim: ISWI's activity is directly regulated by the histone H4 N-terminal tail.
source: ISWI's activity is directly regulated by the histone H4 N-terminal tail and by DNA that flanks the nucleosome, so called linker DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISWI regulation.

claim: ISWI's activity is directly regulated by linker DNA.
source: ISWI's activity is directly regulated by the histone H4 N-terminal tail and by DNA that flanks the nucleosome, so called linker DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISWI regulation.

claim: ISWI can generate arrays of evenly spaced nucleosomes by measuring the length of linker DNA.
source: By measuring the length of linker DNA, ISWI can generate arrays of evenly spaced nucleosomes (Lieleg et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2006; Yamada et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lieleg et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2006; Yamada et al., 2011.

claim: Arrays of evenly spaced nucleosomes are a characteristic feature of chromatin.
source: By measuring the length of linker DNA, ISWI can generate arrays of evenly spaced nucleosomes (Lieleg et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2006; Yamada et al., 2011), a characteristic feature of chromatin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromatin structure.

claim: In compacted chromatin, the histone H4 N-terminal tail of one nucleosome contacts the acidic patch formed by H2A and H2B of a neighboring nucleosome.
source: In the compacted state, the histone H4 N-terminal tail of one nucleosome contacts the acidic patch formed by H2A and H2B of a neighboring nucleosome (Luger et al., 1997; Dorigo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luger et al., 1997 and Dorigo et al., 2004.

claim: Sequestration of the H4 tail by the acidic patch makes it unavailable for binding to and stimulating ISWI activity.
source: This interaction sequesters the H4 tail, which now is no longer available for binding to and stimulating the activity of ISWI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known interaction between H4 tail and acidic patch, and ISWI's dependence on the H4 tail.

claim: ISWI's activity on compacted chromatin would decrease, ensuring unidirectionality of the reaction.
source: Thus, ISWI's activity on the compacted chromatin would decrease, ensuring the unidirectionality of the reaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequestration of the H4 tail in compacted chromatin.

claim: Some ISWI complexes are important in heterochromatin biology.
source: This process is in line with the importance of some ISWI complexes in heterochromatin biology (Bozhenok et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bozhenok et al., 2002.

claim: Evidence points to the ATPase domain of ISWI directly binding the H4 tail.
source: Evidence points to the ATPase domain of ISWI directly binding the H4 tail (Racki et al., 2014; Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Racki et al., 2014 and Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013.

claim: The H4 tail directly influences catalytic reaction steps of ISWI.
source: consistent with the tail directly influencing catalytic reaction steps (Clapier et al., 2001; Dang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clapier et al., 2001 and Dang et al., 2006.

claim: The HAND-SANT-SLIDE (HSS) domain of ISWI has been implicated in binding the H4 tail.
source: However, a domain at the C-terminal side of ISWI, the HAND-SANT-SLIDE (HSS) domain, has been implicated in binding the H4 tail as well (Boyer et al., 2004; Grüne et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2004 and Grüne et al., 2003.

claim: ACF1 associates with ISWI and sequesters the H4 tail under certain conditions.
source: Another layer of regulation is imposed by the non-catalytic subunit termed ACF1, which associates with ISWI and sequesters the H4 tail under certain conditions (Hwang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hwang et al., 2014.

claim: ISWI recognizes amino acids R17H18R19 within the H4 tail, which are part of the basic patch.
source: ISWI recognizes amino acids R17H18R19 within the H4 tail, which are part of a stretch of amino acids called basic patch (Fazzio et al., 2005; Hamiche et al., 2001; Clapier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fazzio et al., 2005; Hamiche et al., 2001; Clapier et al., 2002.

claim: ISWI contains an AutoN motif that is identical to the R17H18R19 motif in the H4 tail.
source: Notably, ISWI contains an identical motif, here called AutoN.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISWI structure.

claim: The 2RA mutation in AutoN increased the DNA-stimulated ATPase activity of ISWI.
source: Mutation of AutoN's two arginines to alanines (referred to as 2RA) increased the DNA-stimulated ATPase activity and nucleosome sliding
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in this study (Figure 8).

claim: The 2RA mutation in AutoN increased nucleosome sliding activity of ISWI.
source: Mutation of AutoN's two arginines to alanines (referred to as 2RA) increased the DNA-stimulated ATPase activity and nucleosome sliding
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in this study (Figure 8).

claim: The 2RA mutation suppressed the dependence of ISWI's ATPase activity on the H4 tail.
source: and suppressed the dependence of ISWI's ATPase and sliding activities on the H4 tail.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in this study (Figure 8).

claim: The 2RA mutation suppressed the dependence of ISWI's sliding activity on the H4 tail.
source: and suppressed the dependence of ISWI's ATPase and sliding activities on the H4 tail.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in this study (Figure 8).

claim: According to the current model, AutoN directly binds to and blocks the H4-tail binding site.
source: According to the current model, AutoN directly binds to and blocks the H4-tail binding site, acting as a gatekeeper for the H4 tail.
evidence: This describes a previous model that is challenged by the current study.

claim: The current model necessitates a conformational change of the NTR to allow binding of H4.
source: This model necessitates a conformational change of the NTR to allow binding of H4 (Hwang et al., 2014; Clapier and Cairns, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hwang et al., 2014 and Clapier and Cairns, 2012.

claim: A conformational change of AutoN upon nucleic acid binding has been observed.
source: Indeed, a conformational change could be traced to AutoN upon nucleic acid binding (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013.

claim: The 2RA mutation diminished but did not abolish H4-tail dependency.
source: Of note, the 2RA mutation diminished but did not abolish the H4-tail dependency, implicating also other regions in the H4 recognition process (Clapier and Cairns, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clapier and Cairns, 2012.

claim: The NTR of ISWI contains an acidic region termed AcidicN.
source: Besides AutoN, the NTR contains additional motifs: an acidic region that we termed AcidicN
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The NTR of ISWI contains the ppHSA motif.
source: the 'post-post-helicase-SANT-associated' (ppHSA) motif, so named because it follows the post-HSA motif in remodelers of the Snf2 family (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013; Szerlong et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013 and Szerlong et al., 2008.

claim: The NTR of ISWI contains a weakly conserved AT-hook.
source: and a weakly conserved AT-hook (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013; Aravind and Landsman, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013 and Aravind and Landsman, 1998.

claim: Multiple sequence alignment of ISWI homologs revealed several sequence motifs in the NTR.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of ISWI homologs revealed several sequence motifs in the NTR of ISWI (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013 and shown in Figure 1.

claim: AutoN is conserved in ISWI homologs.
source: Sequence alignment of these candidates showed conservation of AutoN (Clapier and Cairns, 2012)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ppHSA and AcidicN are at least as conserved as AutoN.
source: but also indicated that two other motifs, termed ppHSA and AcidicN, were at least as conserved (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AT-hook is poorly conserved in ISWI homologs.
source: In contrast, an AT-hook (Aravind and Landsman, 1998) was poorly conserved.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ppHSA is conserved across multiple families of remodelers, including Snf2, Lsh and Ino80.
source: Of note, a separate PSI-BLAST of the NTR of ISWI revealed conservation of ppHSA across multiple families of remodelers, including Snf2, Lsh and Ino80, suggesting shared function (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ppHSA and AcidicN have not been characterized prior to this study.
source: ppHSA and AcidicN have not been characterized so far.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Isw1ΔppHSA did not complement the growth phenotype of the TKO strain at any expression level.
source: In contrast, Isw1ΔppHSA did not complement at any expression level.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Full-length Isw1 fully complemented the growth phenotype of the TKO strain at elevated temperatures.
source: In comparison to a strain lacking only ISW2 and CHD1 (DKO), Isw1WT fully complemented the growth phenotype at elevated temperatures (37°C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: None of the N-terminal truncation variants of Isw1 fully complemented the growth phenotype.
source: Expression of none of the N-terminal truncation variants fully complemented the growth phenotype, indicating functional relevance of the NTR in vivo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isw1 variants that lacked the AutoN-AcidicN region in addition to ppHSA grew modestly better than Isw1ΔppHSA.
source: Isw1 variants that lacked the AutoN-AcidicN region in addition to ppHSA grew modestly better than Isw1ΔppHSA, in line with the general inhibitory nature of AcidicN and AutoN (compare rows 1 and 2 of Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C to the same rows in D; see also below).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All Isw1 mutants showed pronounced toxicity at elevated expression levels.
source: We noted a pronounced toxicity of all Isw1 mutants as indicated by slow growth at elevated expression levels (for instance, compare row four with row five in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Full-length Isw1 was not toxic at comparable expression levels.
source: Full-length Isw1, on the other hand, was not toxic at comparable expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Toxicity at high expression levels could be caused by structural instability of N-terminally truncated Isw1 variants.
source: Toxicity at high expression levels could be caused by structural instability of the N-terminally truncated Isw1 variants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed toxicity and difficulty in purifying analogous ISWI derivatives.

claim: Analogous ISWI derivatives from Drosophila melanogaster proved difficult to purify.
source: Indeed, analogous ISWI derivatives from Drosophila melanogaster proved difficult to purify (see below), supporting the notion that mutations in the NTR destabilize ISWI structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the methods describing various purification strategies.

claim: DNA- and chromatin-stimulated ATPase rates of ISWIΔppHSA and ISWIΔppHSA; ΔAT-hook varied by no more than 1.8-fold from ISWIWT.
source: DNA- and chromatin-stimulated ATPase rates of the truncation mutants varied by no more than 1.8-fold from ISWIWT (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ppHSA and AT-hook are largely dispensable for ATP hydrolysis and proper recognition of chromatin.
source: indicating that ppHSA and AT-hook were largely dispensable for ATP hydrolysis and for proper recognition of chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATPase data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Remodeling activity was affected only modestly by deletion of ppHSA and AT-hook.
source: Remodeling was affected only modestly by deletion of parts of the NTR (3.3- and 1.4-fold for ISWIΔppHSA and ISWIΔppHSA, ΔAT-hook, respectively; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ppHSA and AT-hook are not absolutely required for catalysis in vitro.
source: In conclusion, ATPase and remodeling data suggested that both ppHSA and AT-hook are not absolutely required for catalysis in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATPase and remodeling data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The modest decreases in remodeling activities of ppHSA and AT-hook deletion mutants could be due to lower stability of these enzymes.
source: The modest decreases in remodeling activities could be due to lower stability of these enzymes (see above).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed instability of these mutants.

claim: The NTR might stabilize the structure of ISWI by adopting a similar configuration as the two chromo domains of Chd1.
source: We speculated that the NTR might stabilize the structure of ISWI by adopting a similar configuration as the two chromo domains of the related remodeler Chd1.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural similarities.

claim: The chromo domains of Chd1 are located directly N-terminal to the ATPase module.
source: Like the NTR, the chromo domains are located directly N-terminal to the ATPase module.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chd1 structure.

claim: The chromo domains of Chd1 bridge over and pack against the second ATPase lobe.
source: Notably, they bridge over and pack against the second ATPase lobe, presumably locking the ATPase in an inactive state (Figure 4A) (Hauk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hauk et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ISWIH483B crosslinked to several positions in the NTR within or adjacent to the ppHSA motif.
source: Remarkably, ISWIH483B crosslinked to several positions in the NTR within or adjacent to the ppHSA motif (Figure 1A, arrows; Figure 4C–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The H483B mutation diminished the DNA- and chromatin-stimulated ATPase activity of full-length ISWI by fourfold each.
source: The H483B mutation diminished the DNA- and chromatin-stimulated ATPase activity of full-length ISWI by fourfold each
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The remodeling activity of ISWIH483B was reduced threefold compared to ISWIWT.
source: Importantly, the remodeling activity of ISWIH483B was reduced to a similar degree (threefold), indicating that the efficiency of remodeling per hydrolyzed ATP was unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ISWIH483B efficiently coupled ATP hydrolysis to chromatin remodeling.
source: We conclude that ISWIH483B, albeit hydrolyzing ATP more slowly than ISWIWT, efficiently coupled ATP hydrolysis to chromatin remodeling, which suggested that the mutant remained structurally largely intact.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar fold-reduction in ATPase and remodeling activities.

claim: Auto-regulation of ISWIH483B by its NTR was unperturbed.
source: Also, auto-regulation of ISWIH483B by its NTR was unperturbed because mutagenesis of the NTR had analogous effects on ISWIWT and ISWIH483B (see below), further justifying the use of ISWIH483B for crosslinking experiments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ppHSA motif specifically docked to a location in proximity of amino acid 483 in Lobe 2.
source: We therefore suggest that the ppHSA motif specifically docked to a location in proximity of amino acid 483 in Lobe 2.
evidence: This is inferred from the crosslinking data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Docking of the NTR against Lobe 2 may be necessary for the structural integrity of ISWI-type remodelers.
source: Docking of the NTR against Lobe 2 may be necessary for the structural integrity of ISWI-type remodelers (see above).
evidence: This is speculation based on the instability of NTR deletion mutants.

claim: The presence of ppHSA in other remodelers (Snf2, Lsh and Ino80) predicts similar functions beyond the ISWI family.
source: The presence of ppHSA in other remodelers (Snf2, Lsh and Ino80; Figure 1F) predicts similar functions beyond the ISWI family.
evidence: This is speculation based on sequence conservation shown in Figure 1F.

claim: All three ab initio docking runs yielded a large cluster of models that identified the preferred binding site for AutoN and AcidicN on Lobe 2.
source: All three ab initio docking runs yielded a large cluster of models that identified the preferred binding site for AutoN and AcidicN (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: AcidicN contacted Lobe 2 precisely where an acidic helix of the chromo domains of Chd1 bound.
source: Strikingly, AcidicN, which is predicted to be α-helical (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D), contacted Lobe 2 precisely where an acidic helix of the chromo domains of Chd1 bound (Hauk et al., 2010)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and supported by citation to Hauk et al., 2010.

claim: The NTR adopts a structural architecture akin to the chromo domains of Chd1 despite complete lack of sequence conservation.
source: Based on our results, we propose the NTR to adopt a structural architecture akin to the chromo domains of Chd1 (Figure 4A) despite complete lack of sequence conservation between the two.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the docking and crosslinking data.

claim: Two different H4-tail peptides carrying Bpa at amino acid 1 or 10 were used for crosslinking to ISWI.
source: First, we used two different H4-tail peptides, which carried a Bpa moiety either at amino acid 1 or 10 (T1B and L10B peptides, respectively), and bound these peptides to ISWI26-648 in the presence of DNA (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is described in the Methods section.

claim: UV-irradiation of H4-tail peptides bound to ISWI resulted in crosslinking as indicated by a lower-mobility band on SDS-PAGE.
source: After irradiation, a lower-mobility band was detected by SDS-PAGE, which suggested successful crosslinking (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several crosslinks of the H4 peptides to Lobe 2 were mapped by MS.
source: We mapped several crosslinks of the H4 peptides to Lobe 2 by MS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F; Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: The T1B H4 peptide stimulated the ATPase activity like a wild-type H4 peptide.
source: Control experiments showed that the T1B H4 peptide stimulated the ATPase activity like a wild-type H4 peptide (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Benzophenone-labeled nucleosomes were reconstituted by chemical modification of single cysteine mutants of H4 (T1C and L10C).
source: We reconstituted entire nucleosomes bearing a photo-reactive benzophenone on the N-terminal tail of H4. Benzophenone labeling was achieved by chemical modification of single cysteine mutants of H4 (T1C and L10C).
evidence: This is described in the Methods section.

claim: Benzophenone-labeled nucleosomes bound to full-length ISWI and stimulated its ATPase activity like wild-type nucleosomes.
source: These nucleosomes bound to full-length ISWI and stimulated its ATPase activity like wild-type nucleosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C) suggesting that they were properly recognized by the remodeler.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: UV-irradiation of full-length ISWI bound to benzophenone-labeled T1C nucleosomes retarded the mobility of the remodeler during SDS-PAGE.
source: UV-irradiation of full-length ISWI bound to benzophenone-labeled T1C nucleosomes retarded the mobility of the remodeler during SDS-PAGE, indicative of successful crosslinking (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MS analysis mapped a crosslink between benzophenone-labeled T1C nucleosomes and Lobe 2 of ISWI.
source: MS analysis mapped a crosslink to Lobe 2 of ISWI (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Both T1C- and L10C-labeled nucleosomes crosslinked to Lobe 2 of SNF2H.
source: We repeated these crosslinking experiments with the human ISWI homolog SNF2H. Both T1C- and L10C-labeled nucleosomes crosslinked to Lobe 2 of SNF2H (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–J.

claim: Two very different crosslinking approaches consistently yielded crosslinks between the H4 tail and Lobe 2 of the ATPase domain.
source: In summary, two very different crosslinking approaches, one employing Bpa-containing peptides and one using benzophenone-derivatized nucleosomes, consistently yielded crosslinks between the H4 tail and Lobe 2 of the ATPase domain.
evidence: This is a summary of the crosslinking data shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: Methionine residues were overrepresented as targets of the photo-crosslinking approach.
source: Notably, methionine residues were overrepresented as targets of the photo-crosslinking approach, consistent with the known preference of benzophenones for methionine (Wittelsberger et al., 2006).
evidence: This is noted in the Results section and supported by citation to Wittelsberger et al., 2006.

claim: The H4-tail binding site resides on or close to Lobe 2.
source: In summary, our data strongly indicated the H4-tail binding site to reside on or close to Lobe 2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crosslinking data.

claim: Three or six negatively charged amino acids in AcidicN were replaced by uncharged ones using conservative E to Q and D to N mutations to create ISWI+3 and ISWI+6.
source: To study its function, we replaced three or six negatively charged amino acids in AcidicN by uncharged ones using conservative E to Q and D to N mutations. These mutants were denoted ISWI+3 and ISWI+6 respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is described in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Z2-tag did not interfere with catalytic properties of ISWI.
source: Control experiments ruled out interference of the Z2-tag on catalytic properties of ISWI (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The +3 and +6 mutants had a strongly deregulated ATPase, hydrolyzing ATP markedly faster than ISWIWT when presented with saturating amounts of naked DNA.
source: Of note, the +3 and+6 mutants had a strongly deregulated ATPase, hydrolyzing ATP markedly faster than ISWIWT when presented with saturating amounts of naked DNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DNA-stimulated ATPase rates of ISWI+6 reached values of nucleosome-stimulated ISWIWT rates.
source: In fact, DNA-stimulated ATPase rates of ISWI+6 reached values of nucleosome-stimulated ISWIWT rates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The basal ATPase activity of ISWI+6 was strongly (20-fold) upregulated compared to ISWIWT.
source: Also its basal ATPase activity was strongly (20-fold) upregulated compared to ISWIWT (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Nucleosome-stimulated ATPase and remodeling activities were comparable between the AcidicN mutants and ISWIWT.
source: In contrast to the DNA-stimulated reaction, nucleosome-stimulated ATPase and remodeling activities were comparable between the AcidicN mutants and ISWIWT (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The AcidicN mutants were not simply hyperactive, but misregulated instead.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that the AcidicN mutants were not simply hyperactive, but misregulated instead.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on DNA- vs. chromatin-stimulated activities.

claim: Mutation of AcidicN prevented ISWI from properly recognizing whether chromatin was bound and led to futile ATP hydrolysis in the absence of chromatin.
source: More specifically, mutation of AcidicN prevented ISWI from properly recognizing whether chromatin was bound and led to futile ATP hydrolysis in the absence of chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATPase data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ATP hydrolysis and remodeling were negligible for ISWI+6; E257Q.
source: ATP hydrolysis and remodeling were negligible for ISWI+6; E257Q, providing strong evidence against this possibility (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis was strongly upregulated in the ISWI+3; H483B and ISWI+6; H483B double mutants relative to the ISWIH483B single mutant.
source: DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis was strongly upregulated in the ISWI+3; H483B and ISWI+6; H483B double mutants relative to the ISWIH483B single mutant and reached levels of the chromatin-stimulated reaction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: AcidicN regulates ISWIWT and ISWIH483B in a very similar fashion.
source: We conclude that AcidicN regulates ISWIWT and ISWIH483B in a very similar fashion, further justifying the use of ISWIH483B for crosslinking experiments above.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of AcidicN mutations on both ISWIWT and ISWIH483B.

claim: Three positively charged residues (K403, R458 and R508) in Lobe 2 were selected for mutagenesis to validate the predicted binding interface of AcidicN.
source: We selected three positively charged residues for mutagenesis, K403, R458 and R508, which are predicted to participate in docking to the negatively charged AcidicN motif (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The interface mutants (K403D, R458D, R508D) had a strongly upregulated DNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
source: Indeed, the interface mutants had a strongly upregulated DNA-stimulated ATPase activity whereas chromatin-stimulated ATP turnover and nucleosome remodeling were largely unaffected (Figure 7B,C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The interface mutants behaved just like the AcidicN mutants.
source: The interface mutants therefore behaved just like the AcidicN mutants discussed above.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar phenotypes of interface and AcidicN mutants.

claim: A control mutant (ISWIR486; 488D) retained its ability to discriminate chromatin over DNA in the ATP hydrolysis assay.
source: A control mutant (ISWIR486; 488D), carrying amino acid substitutions just outside of the predicted AcidicN binding interface, however, retained its ability to discriminate chromatin over DNA in the ATP hydrolysis assay (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: AcidicN interacts with Lobe 2 at the predicted interface and this interaction is functionally important to discriminate whether chromatin is bound to the enzyme.
source: These data support the notion that AcidicN interacts with Lobe 2 at the predicted interface and that this interaction is functionally important to discriminate whether chromatin is bound to the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The +3 and +6 ISWI derivatives lost most of their reliance on the H4 tail during remodeling.
source: Strikingly, the +3 and+6 ISWI derivatives lost most of their reliance on the H4 tail during remodeling (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ISWIΔppHSA and ISWIΔppHSA; ΔAT-hook retained a strong H4-tail dependence.
source: In contrast, ISWIΔppHSA and ISWIΔppHSA; ΔAT-hook retained a strong H4-tail dependence, which indicated that ppHSA had little involvement in H4-tail recognition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Two AcidicN interface mutants (K403D and R458D) depended less on the H4 tail during remodeling than ISWIWT.
source: Two AcidicN interface mutants described above (K403D and R458D) also depended less on the H4 tail during remodeling than ISWIWT (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The 2RA mutation suppressed the dependence on the H4 tail in remodeling assays.
source: The 2RA mutation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suppressed the dependence on the H4 tail also in our experiments, albeit our quantitative analysis showed an even more robust reduction than previously seen (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ISWI+6; 2RA barely relied on the presence of the H4 tail.
source: Like the respective single mutants, ISWI+6; 2RA barely relied on the presence of the H4 tail (Figure 8A; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The ISWI+6; 2RA double mutant hydrolyzed ATP even faster in the absence of any ligand compared to the respective single mutants.
source: Compared to the respective single mutants, the ISWI+6; 2RA double mutant hydrolyzed ATP even faster in the absence of any ligand (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Both AcidicN and AutoN motifs contributed to repression of the basal ATPase activity.
source: This result suggested that both motifs contributed to repression of the basal ATPase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect of the double mutation on basal ATPase activity.

claim: DNA- and chromatin-stimulated ATP turnover rates were not further perturbed by the ISWI+6; 2RA double mutation.
source: In contrast, DNA- and chromatin-stimulated ATP turnover rates were not further perturbed by the double mutation (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Both AcidicN and AutoN motifs cooperate during discrimination of chromatin from DNA.
source: consistent with both motifs cooperating during discrimination of chromatin from DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effect of the double mutation on chromatin-stimulated activity.

claim: The H4 tail binds to the conserved Lobe 2 of the ATPase module.
source: Using crosslinking-MS, we found the H4 tail to bind to the conserved Lobe 2 of the ATPase module.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: Direct binding of the H4 tail to the ATPase domain explains regulation of otherwise divergent remodeler families.
source: Direct binding to the ATPase domain explains regulation of otherwise divergent remodeler families
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that the H4 tail binds the ATPase domain.

claim: Direct binding of the H4 tail to the ATPase domain explains the influence of the H4 tail on catalytic steps.
source: and explains the influence of the H4 tail on catalytic, as opposed to purely binding steps (Clapier et al., 2001; Dang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that the H4 tail binds the ATPase domain, supported by citations.

claim: The data do not rule out additional H4 tail binding sites on other domains and on ISWI's partner subunit ACF1.
source: Our data do not rule out additional binding sites on other domains and on ISWI's partner subunit ACF1 as proposed earlier (Boyer et al., 2004; Grüne et al., 2003; Hwang et al., 2014).
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the study and cites previous work.

claim: ISWI and Chd1 proteins have evolved a complex autoregulatory mechanism involving an autoinhibitory domain N-terminal to the ATPase.
source: ISWI and Chd1 proteins have evolved a complex autoregulatory mechanism. This mechanism involves an autoinhibitory domain N-terminal to the ATPase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study and previous knowledge.

claim: Inhibition by the autoinhibitory domain is countered in an unknown fashion by H4-tail binding.
source: Inhibition by this domain is countered in an unknown fashion by H4-tail binding.
evidence: This acknowledges that the mechanism is not fully understood.

claim: In the first model, AutoN acts as a pseudosubstrate by mimicking part of the basic patch of the H4 tail.
source: The first model has been proposed earlier (Clapier and Cairns, 2012) and posits that AutoN acts as a pseudosubstrate by mimicking part of the basic patch of the H4 tail.
evidence: This describes a previous model, supported by citation.

claim: In the first model, the basic patch of the H4 tail must compete with AutoN for the same binding site on the ATPase domain.
source: In this model, the basic patch of the H4 tail must compete with AutoN for the same binding site on the ATPase domain, such that AutoN and possibly the entire NTR is displaced upon tail binding (Clapier and Cairns, 2012; Hauk et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a previous model, supported by citations.

claim: The NTR can in principle undergo conformational changes.
source: This model is supported by the observations that the NTR can in principle undergo conformational changes (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013.

claim: The chromo domains of Chd1 must rearrange before the ATPase domain assumes a catalytically active conformation.
source: and that the chromo domains of Chd1 must rearrange before the ATPase domain assumes a catalytically active conformation (Hauk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hauk et al., 2010.

claim: Direct experimental support for a shared binding site of AutoN and H4 basic patch has been lacking.
source: Direct experimental support for a shared binding site of AutoN and H4 basic patch has been lacking, however
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in previous evidence.

claim: Recent crystallographic evidence did not support the molecular mimicry hypothesis.
source: Recent crystallographic evidence also did not support the molecular mimicry hypothesis (see below) (Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2016.

claim: In the second model, the AutoN and the H4-tail binding sites are not identical, possibly allowing simultaneous binding of both to Lobe 2.
source: We favor a second, simpler model, which does not invoke molecular mimicry (Figure 9). In this model, the AutoN and the H4-tail binding sites are not identical, possibly allowing simultaneous binding of both to Lobe 2 at least temporarily.
evidence: This is the model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The docking sites for the H4 tail and AutoN-AcidicN are adjacent to each other but not overlapping.
source: This scenario is fully compatible with our suggestion that the docking sites for the H4 tail and AutoN-AcidicN are adjacent to each other but not overlapping (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The negatively charged AcidicN motif may promote binding of the basic H4 tail to a neighboring site.
source: Conceivably, the negatively charged AcidicN motif may even promote binding of the basic H4 tail to a neighboring site.
evidence: This is speculation based on the charge complementarity.

claim: The NTR of ISWI docks against Lobe 2 of the ATPase domain in a very similar fashion as the chromo domains of Chd1.
source: Our crosslinking results indicate that the NTR of ISWI docks against Lobe 2 of the ATPase domain in a very similar fashion as the chromo domains of Chd1
evidence: This is based on the crosslinking data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Docking of both NTR and Chd1 chromo domains appears to involve an acidic motif.
source: and docking appears to involve an acidic motif in both cases (Hauk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on the docking data and supported by citation to Hauk et al., 2010.

claim: The overall conformational architecture of ISWI's ATPase module may be shared with Chd1.
source: Thus, the overall conformational architecture of ISWI's ATPase module may be shared with Chd1.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities.

claim: Both NTR and Chd1 chromo domains are known to inhibit the ATPase.
source: Moreover, both domains are known to inhibit the ATPase
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Both NTR and Chd1 chromo domains are predicted to undergo conformational changes upon substrate binding.
source: both are predicted to undergo conformational changes upon substrate binding (Mueller-Planitz et al., 2013; Clapier and Cairns, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Both NTR and Chd1 chromo domains confer sensitivity towards the histone H4 tail.
source: and both confer sensitivity towards the histone H4 tail (Clapier and Cairns, 2012; Hauk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Despite complete lack of sequence conservation between NTR and Chd1 chromo domains, they appear to have evolved very similar functionalities.
source: Thus, despite complete lack of sequence conservation between both domains, they appear to have evolved very similar functionalities.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional and structural similarities.

claim: The ppHSA motif is important for docking the NTR against the ATPase domain.
source: Because the ppHSA motif and adjacent regions crosslinked to the ATPase lobe 2, we suggest that it is important for docking the NTR against the ATPase domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the crosslinking data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ISWIΔppHSA is destabilized in vitro and in vivo.
source: Consistent with such a structural role of this motif, we found that ISWIΔppHSA is destabilized in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The ppHSA motif is present in a wide variety of unrelated remodelers, including Ino80, Lsh, and Snf2.
source: Of note, the ppHSA motif is present in a wide variety of unrelated remodelers, including Ino80, Lsh, and Snf2
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The ATPases of Ino80, Lsh, and Snf2 might bind the ppHSA motif and assemble into a structurally analogous architecture.
source: suggesting that their ATPases, too, might bind the ppHSA motif and assemble into a structurally analogous architecture.
evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation of ppHSA.

claim: ISWI with a mutated AcidicN had a deregulated, hyperactive ATPase activity.
source: In this study, we functionally characterized AcidicN, a novel motif in the NTR. ISWI with a mutated AcidicN had a deregulated, hyperactive ATPase activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: The AcidicN mutant lost its ability to discriminate between DNA and nucleosomes.
source: Notably, this mutant hydrolyzed ATP with comparable velocities when bound to either DNA or nucleosomes, indicating that it lost its ability to discriminate between them.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: The phenotype of AcidicN mutations is reminiscent of mutations in the acidic helix in Chd1.
source: This phenotype is reminiscent of mutations in the acidic helix in Chd1 (Hauk et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hauk et al., 2010.

claim: The effects of AcidicN mutations were remarkably similar to AutoN mutations.
source: The effects of AcidicN mutations were also remarkably similar to AutoN mutations (Clapier and Cairns, 2012), which suggested that they work together.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 and supported by citation.

claim: The mechanism of autoinhibition by the NTR may involve more than simple mimicry of H4's basic patch by AutoN.
source: The mechanism of autoinhibition by the NTR therefore may involve more than simple mimicry of H4's basic patch by AutoN (Clapier and Cairns, 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings about AcidicN and AutoN cooperation.

claim: AcidicN is at least as conserved as AutoN.
source: Supporting its functional importance, AcidicN is at least as conserved as AutoN in our alignments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1.

claim: A crystal structure of the ATPase module of ISWI from a thermophilic fungus became available during revision of the manuscript.
source: During the revision of this manuscript, a crystal structure of the ATPase module of ISWI from a thermophilic fungus became available (Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2016.

claim: The NTR packed against the ATPase domain in the structure of the thermostable ISWI.
source: As suggested by our crosslinking and modeling data, the NTR packed against the ATPase domain in the structure of the thermostable ISWI.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2016.

claim: The authors correctly predicted the AcidicN binding pocket on Lobe 2.
source: We correctly predicted the AcidicN binding pocket on Lobe 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is validated by comparison with the crystal structure from Yan et al., 2016.

claim: The crosslinks between Lobe 2 and the NTR were fully supported by the crystal structure.
source: and our crosslinks between Lobe 2 and the NTR were fully supported by the structure as well.
evidence: This is validated by comparison with the crystal structure from Yan et al., 2016.

claim: The location of the basic patch in the crystal structure overlapped well with the position of the modeled H4 basic patch.
source: Even though only the basic patch of the tail peptide was visible in the structure, its location overlapped well with the position of the modeled H4 basic patch (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and validated by the crystal structure.

claim: AutoN crystallized in closer proximity to the interaction site of the basic patch than suggested by modeling.
source: AutoN crystallized in closer proximity to the interaction site of the basic patch than suggested by modeling
evidence: This is based on comparison with the crystal structure from Yan et al., 2016.

claim: Molecular mimicry of AutoN with the basic patch was not supported by the crystal structure.
source: but molecular mimicry of AutoN with the basic patch was not supported by the structure.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure from Yan et al., 2016.
